n-488b168c: Before we talk about certificates, imagine opening your bank’s website. You have reached a computer. But how do you know it is the computer you intended to reach? That is an identity question. Let’s answer it, one small piece at a time.
n-0094f370: A certificate is like a digital ID card for a server. It carries the server’s name, its public key, and an expiry date. It does not contain the private key. And an ID card is only useful if you can check who issued it.
n-2bbf5cb3: The server also keeps a private key. Think of it as a secret way to prove, this identity belongs to me. A public certificate can be copied. The private key must stay protected. During the connection, the server proves it has that key without sending the key itself.
n-4beb489b: Meet the Certificate Authority, or CA. Think of an office that checks a request and signs an ID card. Its digital signature lets a client detect changes to the certificate. The picture of a stamp is just an analogy. The real signature is mathematical.
n-7d855fc6: Now look at the client, the computer starting the connection. It needs a trusted starting point. With a private CA, you install the CA certificate into the client’s trust configuration. For public websites, browsers already accept selected public roots. A certificate is not trusted just because someone sends it.
n-5d7c8dee: Here is the whole story. Create a key and request a certificate. Have an authorized issuer sign it. Configure what the client trusts. Then the client checks the server, and the TLS handshake establishes encryption. Let’s slow that down and watch the actual files move.
n-402d3d91: Start here. You are the person operating your own Certificate Authority. Think of this as an office that approves and signs server identity cards. This example follows two servers, but a private CA can serve many machines.
n-c6270259: First, create ca.key. This is your CA’s private signing key. Watch it go into the CA’s locked drawer. It stays protected here.
n-ee6abbd2: Next, create ca.crt. It contains the matching public key. This public key lets other computers check your CA’s signatures. The root certificate is self-signed. Creating it does not make everyone trust it.
n-e5c1b9c0: Now look at Server 2. This server needs its own key pair. This is separate from the CA’s key pair.
n-bdd96096: The server’s private key is server-2.key. It stays protected with this server. Later, the server uses it to prove its identity during a connection.
n-02892ef7: The matching public key can be shared. Keep the two owners separate in your mind. The CA signs certificates with ca.key. Server 2 proves its own identity with server-2.key.
n-39aca6a3: Server 2 creates a CSR, a Certificate Signing Request. Look inside: its public key and the server name it wants certified. Server 2 signs the request with its own private key.
n-6346e435: Now follow the request as it travels from Server 2 to your CA. The public key is already inside. There is no need to send it separately.
n-13e543b7: Notice the locked drawer at Server 2. The server’s private key did not travel. The CA receives a request, not the server’s private key.
n-7495cc21: At your CA, first check that this server is allowed to use the requested name. A request by itself is not approval.
n-8491d61c: Your CA creates a server certificate and signs its data with ca.key. Watch the signature appear on server-2.crt. The stamp is a picture for a digital signature, not encryption.
n-097c00fb: Follow the signed certificate back to Server 2. This file is server-2.crt. It is the server’s identity certificate. It is not ca.crt.
n-bbba6a6d: Server 2 now has its own private key and its signed certificate. Inside the certificate are its public key, approved name, dates, and the CA’s signature. The CA did not give Server 2 a replacement private key.
n-022aee66: Now a separate job: client trust. Server 1 acts as the client when it connects to Server 2. You give Server 1 a copy of ca.crt. Follow this public file from your CA to the client.
n-e93ad04a: Receiving the file is not enough. You configure the client to trust this CA certificate. Watch it enter the trusted CA store. The client can now use its public key to verify your CA’s signatures.
n-9c78376d: Pause and compare. The server has its signed identity, server-2.crt. The client trusts the issuer through ca.crt. Issuing a certificate and distributing trust are two separate jobs.
n-0fcf0b1b: Server 1 now connects to Server 2. The CA’s signing key takes no part in this connection. Watch just Server 1 and Server 2.
n-d4a53f06: Server 2 sends its server certificate to Server 1. The file travelling now is server-2.crt. The client already has ca.crt in its trust configuration.
n-08681cf7: During a modern TLS handshake, Server 2 signs handshake data with its own private key. The client checks that proof using the public key in the server certificate. The private key stays locked at the server.
n-01fea50f: Look inside the client’s trusted ca.crt. It contains the CA’s public key. It does not contain a list of server certificates. No search through a list happens here.
n-a566066d: The client uses that trusted CA public key to verify the signature on server-2.crt. These are two different certificates. One gives the verification key. The other carries the signed server identity.
n-97862d87: The client must also check the server name, certificate dates, and allowed purpose. The handshake must prove possession of the matching server private key. A valid signature alone is not enough.
n-4aac26ae: Once verification and the TLS handshake succeed, the peers use negotiated session keys to protect their traffic. The CA signing key stays at the CA. Remember: ca.key signs, ca.crt helps verify, and the server’s own key proves ownership.
n-991be36b: The same idea works for a public website. Your website creates its own private key. It stays protected with the website operator.
n-14e27003: Create a CSR containing the website’s public key and requested domain name. The private key is not inside this request.
n-6851fe4b: Follow server.csr to a public certificate service, such as ZeroSSL. You are asking an external issuer to certify your website identity.
n-0de08c10: The public CA needs evidence that you control the requested domain name. Simply writing a name in a request does not prove that.
n-75371c57: For example, you publish the verification record the CA requests in DNS, or place its verification file on your website. This picture uses a DNS record.
n-0cc98500: The CA checks the published proof. Only after its required checks pass can it approve issuing the certificate. This validates domain control, not whether a website is honest.
n-e863a8f9: The issuing CA signs your website certificate. Public certificate services commonly use an intermediate CA, whose certificate leads to a trusted root.
n-11cb95d0: Follow the server certificate and intermediate certificates back to your website. Your original private key stays with you.
n-6c1b9c58: Install the server certificate, the required intermediate chain, and your matching private key where TLS ends. The certificate and key must match.
n-9ef4833e: The visitor’s browser or operating system already accepts some public roots. That is how it starts with trust, instead of you installing your private CA on every visitor’s device.
n-5afc78d1: Your website presents its certificate and intermediate chain to the browser. Sending these files does not automatically make them trusted.
n-d6a9b25c: The browser verifies the chain to a root it already trusts. It also checks the server name, dates, purpose, and private-key proof. Public trust does not skip these checks.
n-fc957381: After verification and the TLS handshake, protected communication can begin. The main difference is where trust came from. For your internal CA, you configure it. For a public CA, the client may already accept a root in its chain.
n-c8850f56: The certificate was changed after signing. Its signature no longer verifies using the trusted CA public key. The client rejects this identity, even if the server name looks correct.
n-c24960e0: Three roles. The CA private key signs server certificates. The CA certificate gives clients the public key to verify that signature. The server private key proves that the server owns the identity on its certificate.
